title: Response to application from respondent Christa Pike

No. 26A428
CAPITAL CASE
IN THE
Supreme Court of the United States
KENNETH NELSEN, WARDEN
v.
CHRISTA PIKE, 
Movant, 
Respondent.
RESPONSE BRIEF IN OPPOSITION
TO APPLICATION TO VACATE THE STAY
EXECUTION SCHEDULED SEPTEMBER 30, 2026 AT 10:00 A.M. (Central)
FEDERAL DEFENDER 
SERVICES OF EASTERN 
TENNESSEE, INC.
800 S. Gay Street, Suite 2400 
Knoxville, TN 37929
Phone: 865-637-7979 
Fax: 865-637-7999
Email: Luke_Ihnen@fd.org
Luke P. Ihnen, TN BPR No. 035190 *
Stephen Ferrell, TN BPR No. 025170
*Counsel of Record

1 
INTRODUCTION 
The Warden (Movant) seeks to vacate a stay of execution entered by the Sixth 
Circuit Court of Appeals in a case raising grave concerns about the execution of a 
teenaged survivor of child sexual abuse and rape based on a record whose integrity 
was tainted by specious arguments and evidence the State now disavows. Now, a 
panel of the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals has issued a stay of Ms. Pike’s execution 
to weigh whether the federal court should consider Ms. Pike’s motion under Fed. R . 
Civ. P. 60(b)(6). This Court should not intervene.
BACKGROUND
Last month, the State of Tennessee conceded—for the first time—that Christa 
Pike was a teenaged survivor of child sexual abuse and rape who was struggling with 
unmedicated bipolar disorder and PTSD at the time of her crime.1 This was no 
offhand remark in the courthouse hallway. It was an on-the-record, explicit 
concession before a court of law that the state “does not dispute” what happened to 
Ms. Pike.
The importance of that concession cannot be understated. During Ms. Pike’s 
state court post-conviction proceedings, the court discredited Ms. Pike’s history of 
repeated, severe child sexual abuse and rape after the State repeatedly called Ms. 
Pike a “pathological liar” and suggested that she was making up her history of sexual 
1 The transcript reads: “The State does not dispute the terrible things that Ms. Pike 
suffered. I think everybody in this courtroom wishes that those things had never 
happened to Ms. Pike. I think we all wish that we were not here today and that she 
was not on death row…. And so it’s certainly not the State’s intention to try to 
minimize the suffering that Ms. Pike has experienced.” (Aug. 13 Tr. at 82–83) 
Tennessee v. Pike, No. M2020-01156-SC-DPE-DD (Tenn. Aug. 13, 2026).

2 
abuse and rape. The Tennessee Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed the denial of state 
post-conviction relief, Pike v. State, No. E2009-00016-CCA-R3-PD, 2011 WL 1544207, 
at *1 (Tenn. Crim. App. Apr. 25, 2011), based on the post-conviction court’s findings.
Not only that, but the state post-conviction court’s own expression of 
skepticism about the possible impact of the evidence was a reflection of the State’s 
arguments, finding “[t]his lack of credibility with her family members about such 
serious matters could have been a very negative factor for the jury as it related to 
[Christa’s] credibility to other information which she had told other witnesses and 
experts.” Order Denying Post-Conviction Relief, p. 89–90. For the State to now 
recognize that the abuse and its impact were very real certainly impugns the integrity 
of the state court process as well as the habeas court’s careful review of the 
constitutionality of that process.
The federal district court, bound by the AEDPA, also denied relief. Pike v. 
Freeman, No. 1:12-CV-35, 2016 WL 1050717 (E.D. Tenn. Mar. 11, 2016). In 
adjudicating Ms. Pike’s ineffective assistance of counsel claim, that court presumed 
the correctness of the state court’s decision and found that it was neither contrary to 
nor involved an unreasonable application of federal law. See Pike v. Freeman, 2016 
WL 1050717 at **9, 15; 28 U.S.C. §§ 2254(d); 2254(e)(1). The Sixth Circuit Court of 
Appeals affirmed. Pike v. Gross, 936 F.3d 372, 374–75 (6th Cir. 2019). 
On September 29, 2026, Ms. Pike filed a motion to reopen the federal district 
court’s 2016 judgment pursuant to Fed. R . Civ. P. 60(b)(6). The district court 
transferred the motion to the Sixth Circuit pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 2244 to determine

3 
whether Ms. Pike’s motion should be construed as a second or successive habeas 
petition. The Sixth Circuit issued a temporary stay of execution to consider that 
question. This Court must allow it to do so.
ARGUMENT
To grant a stay pending appeal, courts must consider the following factors: (1) 
whether the stay applicant has made a strong showing of the likelihood of success on 
the merits; (2) whether the applicant will be irreparably injured absent a stay; (3) 
whether issuance of the stay will substantially injure the other parties interested in 
the proceeding; and (4) where the public interest lies. Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 
426 (2009). The party seeking the stay—or, in this case, the party seeking to vacate 
the stay—bears the burden of establishing each factor, but the first two are “the most 
critical.” Id. at 433–34. In any event, “[t]he whole idea [of a stay] is to hold the matter 
under review in abeyance” until the appellate court can render “a definitive merits 
decision.” Id. at 432. 
At the very least, this Court should allow the Sixth Circuit to issue its decision. 
Ms. Pike may not ultimately prevail on the merits, but the Respondent has provided 
no compelling grounds to foreclose the Court of Appeals’ consideration of her motion 
under prevailing law. 
I. The Movant is unlikely to succeed on the merits.
The issue before the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals is whether Ms. Pike’s 
60(b)(6) motion should be construed as a subsequent or successive habeas petition 
pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b). The legal question, under Gonzalez v. Crosby, 545

4 
U.S. 524, 532 (2005), is whether Ms. Pike’s 60(b)(6) motion presented a “claim.” 
AEDPA. 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b). 
Rule 60(b) “vests power in courts … to enable them to vacate judgments 
whenever such action is appropriate to accomplish justice.” Klapprott v. United 
States, 335 U.S. 601, 615 (1949). See Plaut v. Spendthrift Farm, Inc., 514 U.S. 211, 
233-34 (1995) (quoting Hazel-Atlas Glass Co. v. Hartford-Empire Co., 322 U.S. 238, 
244 (1944)); see also Tanner v. Yukins, 776 F.3d 434, 438 (6th Cir. 2015) (Rule 60(b) 
“reflects and confirms the courts’ own inherent and discretionary power, ‘firmly 
established in English practice long before the foundation of our Republic,’ to set aside 
a judgment whose enforcement would work inequity.”). See Johnson v. Bell, 605 F.3d 
333, 336 (6th Cir. 2010) (stating that Rule 60(b) “is inherently equitable in nature,” 
and “empowers district courts to revise judgments when necessary to ensure their 
integrity”).
In state post-conviction proceedings, the State presented evidence and 
argument that Ms. Pike was a pathological liar and that her reported history as a 
survivor of sexual abuse was fabricated. The trial court relied on that evidence and 
argument to rule against Ms. Pike, and the federal district court gave deference—as 
it had to do—to the adverse findings. Now, the State agrees that Ms. Pike is not a 
“pathological liar.” Rather, it appears, it was the evidence and argument previously 
presented by the State that was untrue. Now, the State concedes that Ms. Pike was 
repeatedly raped by multiple men from the time she was a toddler until the year

5 
before she committed her crime.2
This self-evidently describes a defect in the prior proceeding, within the 
meaning of Gonzalez v. Crosby, 545 U.S. 524, 532 (2005). At its very foundation, the 
prior proceeding was tainted by the State’s presentation of evidence and argument 
that all parties now agree was untrue. This course of events does not describe a 
“claim” in the sense of a theory as to a particular constitutional right that was 
violated. Instead, they describe a revelation that everything that came before, and 
everything on which the conviction, death sentence, and resolution of prior claims 
stands, no longer exists. The State has now entirely altered its position on the facts 
of the case that it had previously asserted at all stages in the proceeding. Faced with 
this undisputed record, the lower court granted a short stay of execution to allow full 
briefing and measured consideration. And well they should have. Cf. Bennett v. Roper, 
904 F. 3d 623 (8th Cir. 2018); Gonzalez v. Sec’y for Dep’t of Corr., 366 F.3d 1253, 1297 
(11th Cir. 2004) (Tjoflat, J., concurring and dissenting in part) (citing Rodwell v. Pepe, 
324 F.3d 66 (1st Cir. 2003)).
In any case, the issue for this Court is not whether the State’s abrupt and 
complete change of litigation heart amounts to a new claim. The issue is whether the 
Movant has met its heavy burden to vacate a stay. The standard is by now familiar 
2 The State’s about-face also demonstrates the impact the presentation of this 
evidence can have on those who hear it. After hearing Dr. Bethany Brand’s 
compelling testimony, the State’s attorneys recognized the devastating nature of 
child sexual abuse and rape—including its impact on Ms. Pike’s mental health. The 
state post-conviction judge would likely have done the same if the State had not
invoked debunked myths about victims of sexual violence to undermine Ms. Pike’s 
credibility.

6 
and requires, most importantly, “a strong showing of the likelihood of success on the 
merits” and proof that “the applicant will be irreparably injured” absent 
vacatur. Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 426, 433-34 (2009). As noted above, “[t]he 
whole idea [of a stay] is to hold the matter under review in abeyance” until the 
appellate court can render “a definitive merits decision.” Id. at 432. It intends to do 
so.
In its application, the Movant presents no case remotely similar to this. Indeed, 
it presents no cases at all, choosing instead to rely on the dissent below, which 
likewise cited no apposite cases. The absolute least one can say is that the question 
about the meaning of the word, “claim” is unsettled. On this record, one can hardly 
say the Sixth Circuit committed any sort of error, let alone an error sufficient to 
justify the exceptional remedy of vacating a stay.
II. The Movant will not suffer irreparable harm if their motion to vacate 
is denied.
The Respondent will not suffer irreparable harm if its motion is denied. At 
most, Respondent will experience inconvenience. Ms. Pike, by contrast, faces 
execution. The equities weigh heavily in favor of Ms. Pike. 
III. The Movant cannot show that maintaining the stay of execution will 
substantially injure other parties to the proceedings. 
This factor is entitled to less weight under Nken. Nevertheless, the question 
is whether Movant can show “substantial injury.” Ms. Pike agrees that a stay of 
execution is difficult for Ms. Slemmer’s surviving victims. But Ms. Pike’s execution 
would inflict unimaginable pain on her loved ones. Moreover, allowing her execution

7 
to proceed would send a message to survivors of child sexual abuse and other forms 
of sexual violence that their experiences are irrelevant to explaining their life choices 
and actions. It also conveys that parties may invoke debunked myths about the 
credibility of children and teenaged victims of violence to obtain a death sentence, 
then may later retreat from those positions when it is convenient.
IV. The public interest lies with denying the Warden’s motion to vacate 
so that the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals may finish its work.
It is inconceivable that in the 21st century, the criminal justice system is poised 
to execute a survivor of rape and child sexual abuse whose jury never had the 
opportunity to consider those facts in weighing the defendant’s moral culpability. The 
public expects that courts will be fair and reasoned, and that death sentences will be 
carried out only after a process that guarantees that the person facing execution 
receives effective legal representation and fair consideration of all of the evidence 
weighing for and against the appropriateness of capital punishment. That did not 
happen here. 
Hundreds of women’s rights organizations that have spent decades calling for 
justice for survivors of sexual violence have decried the injustice of Ms. Pike’s death 
sentence. See Appendix 1 (Letters from Advocates for Women). The injustice of Ms. 
Pike’s sentence is compounded by her youth at the time of the crime. Scientific 
research has proven that the brains of adolescents do not fully develop until their 
mid-20s. See Appendix 2 (Letters from Youth Justice Advocates). Ms. Pike committed 
her crime on the one-year anniversary of a violent rape, after which she received no 
therapy or victim support services, at a time when she had the brain of an impulsive

8 
and immature teenager struggling with untreated bipolar disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder. That the courts would allow her execution to proceed 
without giving full weight to these facts is unfathomable.
Ms. Pike’s execution would stain the justice system and undermine the public’s 
confidence in its integrity.
V. Ms. Pike did not delay in filing her motion.
Ms. Pike did not deliberately delay the filing of her 60(b) motion, and it was 
not filed for the purpose of delaying the execution. The State’s change of position on 
the credibility of Ms. Pike’s allegations of sexual abuse occurred during the pendency 
of her lethal injection litigation before the Tennessee Supreme Court. That court only 
issued its opinion denying Ms. Pike’s motion on September 23, 2026. This Court 
denied her petition for certiorari on that decision yesterday. She pursued executive 
clemency that was denied on September 28. She did not delay filing her 60(b) motion.

9 
CONCLUSION
For the above reasons Christa Pike asks that this Court deny the State’s 
Application to Vacate the Stay.
 Respectfully submitted,
FEDERAL DEFENDER SERVICES
OF EASTERN TENNESSEE, INC.
